vignette:
Sam presents as a thoughtful and highly intelligent young man, though his posture is perpetually coiled, as if bracing for a phantom impact. At 19, he speaks with the precision of someone much older, a trait that serves him well in his work as a UX designer. He describes his craft with a flicker of his former passion—designing intuitive, predictable pathways for users, creating digital spaces where people feel secure and in control. It’s an irony that is not lost on him.

Six months ago, his own life was a model of such design. Having moved from Lagos to Chicago for a coveted apprenticeship, his world was one of exciting, linear progress. His days were spent mapping user journeys, and his evenings were for exploring a new city that felt boundless. It was during one of these evenings, at a small tech meetup, that he met her. The interaction was brief, a polite exchange over a shared interest in minimalist design. He didn’t think of it again until her first message arrived online, then a second, then a stream of them.

At first, he was just unnerved. He tried to ignore them, then politely disengage. But the digital persistence soon bled into the physical world. She began appearing at the coffee shop where he got his morning latte. He’d look up from his laptop to find her sitting a few tables away, watching. He switched to a different café, but a week later, she was there, too. The city, once boundless, began to shrink.

The fear truly took root when he left his office one night and found a small, hand-carved wooden bird on the windshield of his car. It was a detail he had mentioned in passing during their one and only conversation. This was no longer a coincidence; it was a violation. His world, once governed by logic and predictable inputs, had been hijacked by an irrational variable he couldn't control. He started taking different routes home, varying his schedule, but the feeling of being watched was a constant, humming dread beneath the surface of his thoughts. The climax came on a Tuesday night. A fire alarm in his building forced everyone out onto the street. As he stood shivering in the crowd, he saw her across the way, her gaze fixed on his apartment window. She wasn't a resident. She had no reason to be there. He realized then that she knew where he slept, where he was supposed to be safest.

Though he secured a restraining order and hasn’t seen her in two months, the architecture of his life has been rebuilt around the terror she created. His apartment, once a sanctuary, now feels like a cage with porous walls. Every footstep in the hallway, every creak of the floorboards, sends a jolt of ice through his veins. He triple-checks the deadbolt before bed and has wedged a chair under the doorknob since the night he dreamt she was standing over him, smiling.

At work, his focus is shattered. He will stare at a wireframe on his screen, trying to map a user’s path from a login page to a purchase confirmation, but his mind betrays him. The clean lines of the design morph into the routes he took to avoid her, and a pop-up notification on the screen can make his heart hammer against his ribs, his breath catching in his throat as if he’s just received another one of her messages. He feels a profound sense of shame, a feeling that he somehow invited this, that his initial politeness was a catastrophic design flaw in his own social interface. He has told no one back home; the pressure to be the successful son who made it in America is immense, and this story doesn't fit that narrative. He just feels stuck, trapped in a feedback loop of a terrifying user experience he can’t seem to redesign.
